```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
  fig.width = 11, fig.height = 6.5, dpi = 180, fig.retina = 1, out.width = "100%")
read_results <- function(name) read.csv(file.path(params$gaussian_directory, paste0(name, ".csv")))
conditions <- read_results("conditions")
fits <- read_results("fits") |> left_join(conditions, by = "condition")
selection <- read_results("selection") |> left_join(conditions, by = "condition")
inference <- read_results("inference") |> left_join(conditions, by = "condition")
comparisons <- read_results("comparisons") |> left_join(conditions, by = "condition")
is_pilot <- any(conditions$repetitions < 500L)
complete <- nrow(conditions) == 30L && nrow(fits) == 60L &&
  all(fits$attempted == fits$repetitions)
baseline_methods <- c("always_full", "always_restricted", "lrt_05", "lrt_20")
primary_rows <- function(data) data |>
  filter(method %in% baseline_methods |
    (scenario == "covariance" & method == "check_rank_target") |
    (scenario == "random_slope" & method == "check_rank_any")) |>
  mutate(policy = factor(ifelse(startsWith(method, "check_"), "Check-guided",
    recode(method, always_full = "Full", always_restricted = "Restricted",
      lrt_05 = "LRT .05", lrt_20 = "LRT .20")),
    levels = c("Full", "Restricted", "LRT .05", "LRT .20", "Check-guided")))
axis_labels <- c(stable_cor = "Stable correlation", occasion_cor = "Occasion correlation",
  occasion_sd_ratio = "Occasion SD ratio", random_slope = "Random-slope SD")
parameter_labels <- c(x_actor = "Actor slope", x_partner = "Partner slope",
  x_actor_between = "Actor between", x_actor_within = "Actor within",
  x_partner_between = "Partner between", x_partner_within = "Partner within",
  role_average_intercept = "Average intercept", role_difference = "Role difference")
interval <- function(rate, lower, upper) sprintf("%.1f%% [%.1f, %.1f]", 100 * rate, 100 * lower, 100 * upper)
primary <- primary_rows(inference)
primary_selection <- primary_rows(selection)
primary_comparisons <- primary_rows(comparisons)
```

## Question and design

When a covariance restriction is wrong, can a fixed model-selection rule protect
inference for the effects we care about? This study compares **always using the
full model**, **always using the restricted model**, likelihood-ratio selection
at **.05 or .20**, and **selection using the dependence check**. A significant
comparison or a diagnostic flag retains the full model.

The output contains `r sum(fits$attempted)` fit attempts across
`r nrow(conditions)` conditions, targeting `r unique(conditions$repetitions)`
datasets per condition.
`r if (!complete) "**These results are incomplete. Missing attempts must be resolved before drawing conclusions.**" else if (is_pilot) "**These are pilot results for checking the workflow. They do not establish error rates or support a model-selection recommendation.**" else "The results apply to the simulated settings, not every model supported by the package."`

The 24 covariance conditions reuse the completed
[longitudinal consequences study](ild-partner-dependence.html): 50 or 200 dyads,
14 complete occasions, stable correlations 0/.1/.2/.4, occasion correlations
0/.1/.2/.3, or occasion SD ratios 1/1.1/1.25/1.5. Each condition changes one
feature. Full and restricted models are refitted from the same saved seeds to
obtain their likelihoods. Saved diagnostic references are reused only after
checking source and software provenance and reproducing estimates and SEs.
Predictors are generated independently between partners at both levels.

Six new conditions use the same sample sizes and occasions, with independent
member-specific actor-within random-slope SDs of 0/.2/.5. The fixed effects
separate actor and partner predictors into member means and within-member
deviations. The restricted model omits the random slope.

<details>
<summary>Selection rules, null effects and limitations</summary>

For covariance restrictions, check-guided selection uses the corresponding
partner-correlation row (between or within), or the within average/difference
correlation for equal occasion SDs. Rank limits are primary. Selecting on any
row and the older quantile limits are saved sensitivity analyses. There is no
random-slope-specific row: its conditions use any of the 12 rows to test the
limits of the existing check.

All models use maximum likelihood and the same fixed-effect terms within each
comparison. Covariance restrictions remove one interior parameter. Removing
the independent random-slope variance uses the asymptotic equal mixture of a
point mass at zero and chi-square with one degree of freedom; other covariance
parameters remain interior in the generating model. The zero-slope conditions
assess its small-sample behavior. This is not a general rule for deleting
correlated random-effect blocks. See [Self and Liang (1987)](https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1987.10478472).
Comparing .05 with .20 follows the selection question in
[Matuschek et al. (2017)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jml.2017.01.001), without
assuming that either threshold transfers safely to these models.

True-zero scientific effects are obtained by subtracting the true fixed-effect
mean, *Xβ*, from each Gaussian response. Both candidates retain the same fixed
design matrix. This shifts coefficient estimates by their true values, while
leaving covariance likelihoods, SEs and model-centred checks unchanged. The
pilot verifies this within numerical tolerance with actual shifted-response
refits and new simulations, and checks that inference and selection decisions
are unchanged.
The null and nonzero cases are therefore **matched transformations of the same
datasets**, not additional independent datasets. This argument does not apply
to generalized models.

Coverage describes whether a 95% Wald interval contains the known true effect.
Null rejection is the false-positive rate; rejection under the nonzero effects
is power. Under the exact Gaussian translation used here, null rejection equals
one minus nonzero coverage. A high power near 100% provides little information
about differences between methods; this study does not vary scientific effect
sizes to compare their whole power curves.

</details>

## Fit availability and fallback

A candidate must have optimizer convergence, a positive-definite Hessian, a finite
likelihood and defined estimates and SEs. A full model whose log-likelihood is
more than 0.000001 below that of its usable nested restriction is excluded from
every selection rule, even if its optimizer and Hessian checks passed. Original fit status and
estimates are preserved. If only one candidate is eligible,
selection methods use it and count a **fallback**. If neither is eligible they
return no inference. If both are eligible but a comparison or check is undefined,
that rule also returns no inference.

The always-full and always-restricted baselines return no inference when their
specified model is unavailable. Thus availability and fallback must be read
alongside interval performance. Rates below use all returned usable estimates;
the saved tables also give results restricted to datasets with both models
usable. No results are conditioned on a missing flag.

```{r availability}
availability <- fits |>
  summarise(Attempted = sum(attempted), Usable = sum(inference_defined),
    .by = c(axis, n_dyads, fit)) |>
  mutate(Result = paste0(Usable, "/", Attempted)) |>
  select(axis, n_dyads, fit, Result) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = fit, values_from = Result) |>
  mutate(Restriction = unname(axis_labels[axis])) |>
  select(Restriction, Dyads = n_dyads, Full = full, Restricted = restricted)
knitr::kable(availability, caption = "Eligible fits with defined inference across strengths within each design; counts retain all attempted datasets.")
```

```{asis, echo=!is_pilot && complete}
Of 30,000 fits, 29,999 passed the optimizer and Hessian checks, and 29,532
were eligible after excluding 467 full fits with lower nested likelihoods.
At true-zero slope variance, only 317/500 full fits were eligible at 50 dyads
and 230/500 at 200 dyads. Their always-full rates describe selected subsets;
the selection rules returned all 500 datasets using their stated fallback.
A bounded review reproduced three near-zero-slope likelihood reversals and a
nonreversed control. Full and restricted estimates differed by less than 0.002
SE, and their SEs by less than 0.06%. One alternative optimizer did not resolve
the reversals. It did resolve the separate Hessian failure. These checks do not
establish global maxima; all original exclusions remain in the results.
```

<details>
<summary>Returned inferences and fallback counts by rule</summary>

```{r policy-availability}
primary_selection |>
  summarise(Attempted = sum(attempted), Returned = sum(returned),
    Fallback = sum(fallback), `Full selected` = sum(full_selected),
    .by = c(axis, policy)) |>
  mutate(Restriction = unname(axis_labels[axis])) |>
  select(Restriction, Rule = policy, everything(), -axis) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Counts pooled over sample sizes and strengths for availability only; they are not pooled error-rate estimates.")
```

</details>

## False positives after selection

The plot uses prespecified example targets: the average intercept for the two
correlation restrictions, the actor slope for SD pooling, and the actor-within
slope for random-slope removal. The table below includes every target. Dashed
lines mark 5%; error bars are 95% Wilson intervals across simulated datasets.
These intervals measure Monte Carlo uncertainty, not uncertainty about a
particular observed dataset.

```{r null-rejection, fig.alt="Null rejection rates for five model selection rules, across restriction strengths and 50 or 200 dyads."}
focus <- primary |>
  filter(sample == "all", effect_case == "null",
    (axis %in% c("stable_cor", "occasion_cor") & parameter == "role_average_intercept") |
    (axis == "occasion_sd_ratio" & parameter == "x_actor") |
    (axis == "random_slope" & parameter == "x_actor_within")) |>
  mutate(Design = factor(axis, names(axis_labels),
    paste0(axis_labels, "\n", c("Average intercept", "Average intercept", "Actor slope", "Actor within"))),
    Dyads = factor(paste(n_dyads, "dyads"), levels = c("50 dyads", "200 dyads")))
ggplot(focus, aes(strength, rejection, colour = policy, group = policy)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = 2, colour = "grey55") +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = rejection_lower, ymax = rejection_upper), width = 0,
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.025), alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.025), size = 1.8) +
  facet_grid(Dyads ~ Design, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(), limits = c(0, NA)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#333333", "#D55E00", "#0072B2", "#009E73", "#CC79A7")) +
  labs(x = "True correlation, SD ratio or random-slope SD", y = "Null effects declared significant",
    colour = NULL, caption = if (is_pilot) "Pilot only: these rates do not establish calibration." else NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

<details>
<summary>Coverage and power for all targets at the largest restriction</summary>

This table uses the largest simulated correlation, SD ratio or slope SD within
each design. Full tables also retain every smaller strength. Brackets are 95%
Monte Carlo intervals. The scientific effects are nonzero here.

```{r coverage-power}
primary |>
  filter(sample == "all", effect_case == "nonzero") |>
  filter(strength == max(strength), .by = axis) |>
  mutate(Design = unname(axis_labels[axis]), Target = unname(parameter_labels[parameter]),
    Coverage = interval(coverage, coverage_lower, coverage_upper),
    Power = interval(rejection, rejection_lower, rejection_upper)) |>
  arrange(axis, n_dyads, parameter, policy) |>
  select(Design, Dyads = n_dyads, Target, Rule = policy, n, Coverage, Power) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>Paired coverage changes relative to the full model</summary>

These secondary comparisons use datasets where both candidates were usable.
They isolate the change in coverage within the same datasets. Intervals are
the change plus or minus 1.96 Monte Carlo SEs, in percentage points.

```{r paired-changes}
primary_comparisons |>
  filter(effect_case == "nonzero", method != "always_full") |>
  filter(strength == max(strength), .by = axis) |>
  filter((axis %in% c("stable_cor", "occasion_cor") & parameter == "role_average_intercept") |
    (axis == "occasion_sd_ratio" & parameter == "x_actor") |
    (axis == "random_slope" & parameter == "x_actor_within")) |>
  mutate(Design = unname(axis_labels[axis]),
    Change = sprintf("%+.1f [%+.1f, %+.1f]", 100 * coverage_change,
      100 * (coverage_change - 1.96 * coverage_change_mcse),
      100 * (coverage_change + 1.96 * coverage_change_mcse))) |>
  select(Design, Dyads = n_dyads, Rule = policy, n, Change) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

</details>

## What this can support

```{asis, echo=!is_pilot && complete}
- **The dependence checks missed consequential random slopes.** At slope SD
  0.5, omitting the slope gave actor-within false-positive rates of 22.2% and
  25.0% at 50 and 200 dyads. Check-guided selection always chose that restricted
  model. Full models and both LRT rules gave 6.0% and 5.0%. At 200 dyads, the
  respective 95% Monte Carlo intervals were 21.4–29.0% and 3.4–7.3%.
- **A detectable covariance difference need not greatly affect these targets.**
  At 200 dyads, an occasion correlation of 0.1 and an SD ratio of 1.1 were flagged
  in 99.6% and 99.8% of datasets. Yet paired full-versus-restricted coverage
  differences across the occasion covariance and SD conditions were at most
  1.4 percentage points.
- **Model comparison helped, within these designs.** LRT selection limited
  false positives from omitted slopes and recovered much of the power lost by
  omitting stable correlation. Coverage estimates have Monte Carlo uncertainty;
  the paired comparisons above quantify uncertainty in their differences.
  These results do not establish nominal coverage in general, a universally
  preferable LRT threshold, or a general power advantage from simplification.

The random-slope result concerns the partner-dependence check. It does not
establish whether predictor-specific residual checks would detect that omission.
```

This study evaluates the **whole prespecified procedure**, including numerical
failures and fallback, rather than treating a nonsignificant comparison or an
unflagged check as proof that simplification is harmless. Its results can support
bounded advice about the tested Gaussian models. They cannot establish an
automatic simplification rule for arbitrary random-effect structures,
generalized models, or searches over different role definitions.

Covariance pooling also does not establish equality of role-specific means or
slopes. No flag, or a nonsignificant model comparison, is not evidence of
equivalence. Inspect the estimates, SEs and intervals for the scientific effects
across feasible models, and report unresolved sensitivity.

The saved CSV tables contain all strengths and targets, bias, empirical SD,
model SE accuracy, Wilson intervals, Monte Carlo SEs, availability, and the
paired and flag-rule sensitivities. The runner and validation checks are in
`dev/diagnostic_checks/simulation-studies/model-simplification/`.
